cases.title: Eagle Avenue Lift Bridge
cases.summary: The two exposed counterweights, freestanding braced towers and narrow mast over the span form a distinctive match between the film and a separately labeled historical photograph. The evidence identifies the bridge visible in frames 638 and 652; it does not locate the camera or the gravel pile precisely.

frames.caption: Frame 652 gives the clearest combined view of both braced lift towers, their broad rectangular counterweights and the thin mast between them.
frames.alt: Frame 652 gives the clearest combined view of both braced lift towers, their broad rectangular counterweights and the thin mast between them.

references.caption: The source independently labels this as the Eagle Street lift bridge. The exposed counterweights, open braced towers and central lattice mast are the features used in this comparison. The photograph is taken from a vessel at a different angle.
references.alt: Black and white view of the Eagle Street lift bridge from a vessel, showing the truss span, exposed counterweights at the towers and a narrow mast above the span.

observations.title: Paired towers and counterweights
observations.text: Frame 652 shows two tall, freestanding steel towers with open diagonal bracing and unusually broad, exposed rectangular counterweights. The labeled reference has the same arrangement. This combination carries more identifying weight than the general industrial setting.

observations.title: The narrow mast between the towers
observations.text: A thin lattice mast rises above the span in both frame 652 and Figure XIII, with lines extending toward the towers. It adds a second, spatially related feature to the tower comparison.

observations.title: A link between two film views
observations.text: The braced tower and broad counterweight behind Tank in frame 638 are consistent with the clearer pair in frame 652. The identification applies to these visible structures; adjacent cuts in the sequence still need their own evidence.

uncertainties: The historical photograph's capture date and individual photographer are not specified in the chapter. The 1981 date belongs to the book, and 2016 belongs to the digital edition.
The film and reference use different viewpoints. Neither the precise camera station nor the gravel-pile parcel is established.
The map point marks the bridge as a landmark. It does not trace Tank's route or assign every nearby industrial insert to this site.
cases.resolution: Retain Eagle Avenue Lift Bridge as a strong landmark identification for frames 638 and 652. A period site plan or aerial tied to the film's sight lines would be needed to locate the gravel pile and camera more precisely.

observations.title: A named architectural candidate
observations.text: The film's MADISON lettering is unusually useful. The long brick elevation, pale corner blocks, stacked balconies and central arch provide several features that a complete historical facade photograph could test together.

observations.title: Partial corner correspondence
observations.text: The 1964 photograph independently fixes a drugstore corner at Hough Avenue and East 79th Street. Its pale corner blocks and Coca-Cola cornice support the comparison with frame 63, but the reference includes only a narrow part of the candidate building.

observations.title: Two address forms on one named frontage
observations.text: The municipal inventory lists Madison Square at 7812–14 Hough; the 1943–44 and 1955 apartment directories use 7820. Hopkins plate 6b, dated 1921 and revised in 1924, labels MADISON SQUARE BLDG. on the southwest corner with Hough frontage numbers 7812–7828. Both address forms fall within that named building frontage. The map does not say which doorway served the apartments.

observations.title: Later block context
observations.text: The 1972 aerial helps place the intersection within the surrounding blocks. It should be read with its date and oblique angle in mind when comparing it with the film's street-level view.

uncertainties: A source photograph showing the central arch, the entire balcony pattern and the roof lettering together has not yet been matched.
The map reconciles the address forms at building level. The apartment entrance and individual storefront functions are not assigned by the plat labels.
The SQUARE portion of the film's roof lettering is less legible than MADISON in the available 480 × 270 still.
The corner photograph dates to 1964 and the aerial to 1972; neither is a documented film-production photograph.

Approximate Madison Square Building site, southwest corner of Hough Avenue and East 79th Street. Placement follows the historic plat-map mosaic; allow roughly 30 m of positional uncertainty as a working allowance. This is a building-site marker, not a film camera position. Frames 58–62 remain unassigned.
cases.resolution: Keep the film identification probable. Seek a dated full Hough Avenue facade photograph or building elevation for Madison Square, 7812–7828 Hough, that can test the central arch, complete balcony arrangement, roof lettering and corner storefront together.

cases.title: Former Clark Avenue Bridge and furnace views
cases.summary: A newly located 1984 county photograph looks directly through the former Clark Avenue Bridge’s central truss. The haunched transverse frames and dense crossed overhead lattice closely match frame 658, materially strengthening the candidate. The dismantled deck leaves the intact roadway, skyline and camera position unresolved. Clark remains probable and unpinned.

observations.title: A direct view through the central truss
observations.text: Fuerst’s 1984 cea0146 photograph looks along the central truss during deck demolition. Repeated transverse frames with haunched upper corners, dense crossed bracing overhead, a broad far opening and riveted side members closely correspond with frame 658. These repeating internal frames are not separate bridge spans.

observations.title: The remaining roadway comparison
observations.text: The new photograph materially strengthens the structure comparison, but its removed deck and centered viewpoint differ from the film. An in-service view, preferably near 1968, is still needed to align the road edge, railing, sequence of internal frames and industrial skyline. The earlier cea0144 photograph supplies a separate view from below.

observations.title: Correcting the tall structure in frame 654
observations.text: The close view shows industrial piping and furnace equipment alongside grouped stacks. This feature belongs to the furnace complex and cannot serve as evidence for a lift-bridge tower.

observations.title: A documented industrial setting
observations.text: The 1935 archive caption places Republic Steel furnaces beside Clark Avenue Bridge. It supports the general setting of the candidate. The different date and view do not identify the film's exact furnace, steel-company parcel or camera station.

observations.title: The old roadway is gone; its history needs precise dates
observations.text: The original road deck cannot be visited. County Engineer photographs document demolition in 1984 and 1985. A 1918 account gives the complete crossing as 6,687 feet including fills, with 5,992 feet of steelwork. The later engineering history’s acid-fume passage concerns Harvard–Denison. The exact October 16, 1978 closure date and the proposed pollution explanation have not been established from a primary Clark record in this check. ODOT dates the I-490 valley bridge to 1990.

observations.title: The supplied pier coordinate fails the aerial check
observations.text: Latitude 41.472714, longitude −81.681121 falls on an industrial building roof at the center of the checked 2019 county aerial. It is not a verified location for the two proposed piers. No replacement pier or film-camera coordinate is assigned. A surviving foundation would still require a separate match to the filmed roadway.

uncertainties: The central-truss framework now has a close historical comparison. The intact road edge, railing and complete industrial skyline have not yet been aligned in one in-service view.
Both 1984 county photographs record demolition after the film; removed or changed elements limit comparison with the operating bridge.
The film's precise camera stations, furnace identity and steel-company parcel remain unresolved.
The transition from Eagle Avenue in frame 652 to the furnace views does not by itself establish a continuous route or shared shooting position. Other ore-yard inserts retain their separate status.

An east-facing camera bearing and the exact Republic Steel furnace alignment remain unverified. Frame 658 does not locate every subsequent industrial cut. The supplied pier coordinate is not a verified bridge-remnant or camera point.
Present-day public access to any surviving foundations has not been verified. Exact closure and final demolition days remain historical research leads.
cases.resolution: Retain the former Clark Avenue Bridge as probable and unpinned. Seek an in-service roadway photograph, preferably near 1968, that aligns the road edge, railing, internal frame sequence and industrial skyline. Frames 653–654 still need their own direct furnace-equipment comparison.

cases.title: Carter Road and the adjacent railroad lift bridge
cases.summary: Frame 639’s broad Carter Road tower with a notched crown, narrower adjacent railroad tower and approach-road setting closely match a labeled July 1986 HAER photograph. The comparison identifies Carter Road Lift Bridge with the adjacent Big Four / New York Central railroad lift bridge. The southeast-facing archive view favors the northwest approach side. The exact film camera position, foreground street and overhead structure remain unverified; the proposed Columbus Road underpass is not established.

frames.caption: The broad, notched highway tower is at left, with the narrower railroad lift tower immediately to its right. An unidentified overhead girder and support frame the street-level view.
frames.alt: Frame 639: two adjacent lift bridges seen beneath a dark overhead girder, with a broad notched tower at left and a narrow tower at right.

references.title: Carter Road Lift Bridge and Cleveland, Columbus, Cincinnati, and St. Louis Railroad Bridge Number 5
references.credit: Barrow, William C.; Graduate Assistant Collection; Cleveland Memory Project.
references.rights: The archive links to Cleveland Memory’s copyright guidance; no open license is asserted here. Photograph by William C. Barrow, CSU Graduate Assistant Collection.
references.caption: A May 2002 broadside view explicitly catalogued as the Big Four railroad lift in front of Carter Road Bridge. The later photograph confirms the relationship between the two structures; it does not establish their 1968 operating condition.

observations.title: Two different tower profiles, in the same arrangement
observations.text: The stepped crown and broad open cross-bracing of the left tower correspond with Carter Road in the labeled 1986 photograph. The narrower railroad tower is immediately to its right in both images. The combined silhouettes and their relationship provide a stronger identification than a general lift-bridge resemblance.

observations.title: The approach favors a southeast-facing view
observations.text: The HAER caption explicitly says looking southeast. The film’s matching left/right tower arrangement and approach-road setting favor a view from the northwest approach side. A triangular road sign supplies supporting context, without establishing that the same sign survived between 1968 and 1986.

observations.title: The overhead structure is a separate question
observations.text: The film includes a dark girder across the top and a heavy support at right. The comparison photograph does not show these features. It therefore cannot identify the overhead structure as Columbus Road Bridge or a particular railway overpass, or establish an exact street-level camera station.

observations.title: Keep the film date separate from later bridge history
observations.text: The 2002 archive view independently labels the adjacent road and Big Four railroad bridges. A Conrail map dated April 1, 1981 lists the River Bed Main Line under anticipated abandonment. Neither source establishes the railroad’s operating status in 1968; “abandoned” is not used as a film-period description.

observations.title: Modern riverfront viewpoints
observations.text: The Canalway’s current trailhead list gives Scranton Flats at 2057 Scranton Road and Sokolowski’s Overlook at 1203 University Road. These can orient a present-day visit, but neither is established as the camera location. The proposed Superior Viaduct viewpoint has not been checked for this exact sight line.

uncertainties: The HAER photograph was made in July 1986, eighteen years after the film, and uses different framing. The broad bridge-pair identification is strong; the inferred viewing direction is less precise.

The southeast-facing archive view favors the northwest approach side. The exact film camera position, foreground street and overhead structure remain unverified; the proposed Columbus Road underpass is not established.
The comparison photographs date to 1986 and 2002. A 1981 Conrail map lists anticipated abandonment of the River Bed Main Line; no verified abandonment date or 1968 operating status is assigned here.
More than one Big Four / New York Central lift bridge crossed this part of the river. The adjacent Carter pair must not inherit dates, engineering details or bridge numbers from another crossing.
Frames 640–641 and later industrial cuts require their own landmark comparisons. Editing does not establish a continuous route.
The existing point marks the Carter Road bridge landmark; it is not a camera coordinate or a verified place to recreate the shot.
cases.resolution: Identify the visible Carter Road and adjacent railroad lift bridges with strong visual confidence. Treat a southeast-facing view from the northwest approach as an inference, and leave the exact overhead structure and camera point open. A period approach plan and a labeled underpass view would help settle those remaining features.

researchNotes.remaining: The scene stays unplaced. researchNotes.topic: Carter Road: a labeled southeast approach comparison
researchNotes.checked: Compared frame 639 with Louise Taft Cawood’s July 1986 HAER approach photograph and William C. Barrow’s May 2002 bridge-pair view. Checked the river-crossing inventory, original Conrail 1981 map and official modern trailhead listings.
researchNotes.found: Frame 639’s broad Carter Road tower with a notched crown, narrower adjacent railroad tower and approach-road setting closely match a labeled July 1986 HAER photograph. The comparison identifies Carter Road Lift Bridge with the adjacent Big Four / New York Central railroad lift bridge. The archive caption supports a southeast-facing approach; the broad and narrow tower profiles make the landmark identification strong.
researchNotes.remaining: The southeast-facing archive view favors the northwest approach side. The exact film camera position, foreground street and overhead structure remain unverified; the proposed Columbus Road underpass is not established. The comparison photographs date to 1986 and 2002. A 1981 Conrail map lists anticipated abandonment of the River Bed Main Line; no verified abandonment date or 1968 operating status is assigned here. Modern trailheads and the proposed Superior Viaduct overlook are not verified recreations of this shot.

researchNotes.topic: Additional riverfront claims: hotel, concrete arches and ore gantry
researchNotes.checked: October 18 follow-up: compared the supplied attribution with the actual indexed stills and the identified institutional or archival records.
researchNotes.found: Frame 602’s taller hotel does not fit Flat Iron Cafe’s official address and two-story building history. B&O No. 463 is a probable background bridge. Frame 646 supports Detroit–Superior, with a probable Union Terminal viaduct behind. Frame 667 shows ore-handling machinery, not the proposed river bridge.
researchNotes.remaining: The hotel name, its HOTEL sign’s origin, the exact approach arch in frame 646 and the ore-yard parcel remain unresolved. The supplied precise recreation points are not established.

sources.title: Flat Iron Cafe: official address and building history
sources.note: The cafe lists 1114 Center Street and says a late-nineteenth-century fire reduced its former hotel building to two stories. This conflicts with the supplied 1633 West 2nd address and the taller hotel in frame 602. The business history supplies no film-production or temporary HOTEL-sign evidence.

sources.title: Glenn Zahn: B&O Bridge No. 463 under construction, July 3, 1956
sources.note: Cleveland Press photograph, clevbridge015.jpg; Cleveland Memory urbanohio/203. The catalog identifies B&O No. 463 and its jackknife-bascule construction. The 1956 bridge replaced a Scherzer rolling lift; it is distinct from the New York Central / Penn Central vertical lift called Bridge No. 1.

sources.title: William C. Barrow: Baltimore and Ohio Bridge Number 463, May 16, 2002
sources.note: Cleveland Memory urbanohio/413, gacbridge053, Graduate Assistant Collection. The upright long leaf and articulated triangular mechanism provide a probable silhouette comparison for the distant bridge in frame 602. This later opposite-bank view does not identify the hotel or camera point.

sources.title: Jet Lowe: Detroit–Superior east-approach concrete arch, 1978
sources.note: HAER photograph, Library of Congress; Cleveland Memory urbanohio/459. The catalog identifies an east-approach arch. Similar concrete arch construction is therefore insufficient by itself to assign frame 646 to the west approach or a particular street corner.

sources.title: Bridges of Metropolitan Cleveland: railroad viaducts
sources.note: Describes the Cleveland Union Terminal Railway Bridge directly south of Detroit–Superior; supports the geographic inference in frame 642.

researchNotes.topic: United Electric and Leader Drug: new address claims remain unplaced
researchNotes.checked: October 18 follow-up: compared the supplied attribution with the actual indexed stills and the identified institutional or archival records.
researchNotes.found: United Electric and Leader Drug are visible business names. No retrieved period record or matching photograph supports 3630 Euclid for frame 331 or Hough / East 79th for frame 169. The later United Electric premises at East 23rd does not match the lighting showroom.
researchNotes.remaining: Match each 1968 business frontage before assigning an address or demolition history. The prior Kronheim and Leader directory controls remain dated leads.

sources.title: United Electric Fixture & Supply Co. v. United Electric Supply Co., 1956
sources.note: Court decision reproduced online distinguishes businesses at 1772 East 9th and 5805 Euclid. It does not settle the 1968 storefront address.

sources.title: Richard Van Curen: United Electric premises at 1830 East 23rd, 1979
sources.note: CSU Office of Campus Planning photograph, Cleveland Memory structure/585. This later industrial facade does not reproduce frame 331’s lighting showroom. It does not establish a 1968 address or corporate continuity with either firm in the 1956 court record.

sources.title: Cleveland City Directory, 1955, printed page 729
sources.note: Kronheim furniture retail listing at 2041 East 55th Street. A historical lead only; no 1968 Leader Drug pairing established.

sources.title: Cleveland City Directory, 1974: Kronheim entries, printed p. 544
sources.note: Original scan, CPL leaf 60736, parent volume 61902; the title leaf 59919 confirms 1974 Cleveland proper. Kronheim’s is listed at 2043 East 55th, with a furniture branch at 15204 Puritas and furniture or related offices at 1814 East 40th. Later evidence only; no 1968 pharmacy adjacency is established. Street digits were checked visually against the scan.

sources.title: Cleveland City Directory, 1974: Leader entries, printed p. 566
sources.note: Original scan, CPL leaf 60759, parent volume 61902. Alphabetical Leader entries list Leader Drug at 1400 East 9th and 5909 Broadway, Leader Discount Drug at 11650 Detroit, and Leader Drug–Kamm’s Plaza at 17400 Lorain. These 1974 entries are neither a 1968 branch list nor a demonstrated complete list of affiliates using other trade names.

researchNotes.topic: East Side churches and street routes: separate history from filming evidence
researchNotes.checked: October 18 follow-up: compared the supplied attribution with the actual indexed stills and the identified institutional or archival records.
researchNotes.found: Cory’s address at 1117 East 105th and its civil-rights role are documented, but no shot has been matched to it. The present St. Agnes / Our Lady of Fatima complex dates to 1983; its two predecessor parishes were separate in 1968. Madison’s probable frame 63 identification still rests on the roof lettering, partial facade and historical footprint.
researchNotes.remaining: Identify a specific shot for Cory, either predecessor church, East 79th / Lexington, or a Hough East 55th–East 79th street route. No continuous procession route, unchanged street grid or present-day recreation point is established. The opening Atlanta funeral sequence retains its separate location.

sources.title: St. Agnes + Our Lady of Fatima: parish history
sources.note: The parish places St. Agnes at East 79th and Euclid, with a 1917 church demolished in 1975. Our Lady of Fatima was established separately on Lexington in 1949. The parishes merged in 1980 and the present adjacent complex was dedicated April 16, 1983. A 1968 film claim must identify a predecessor building; no specific shot has been matched.

sources.title: National Park Service: Cory United Methodist Church
sources.note: Institutional history documents Cory’s civil-rights organizing and community role. It does not establish an appearance in Uptight. The separate municipal landmark record confirms the address at 1117 East 105th Street.

sources.title: City of Cleveland: Cory United Methodist Church landmark
sources.note: Municipal landmark identity and address: 1117 East 105th Street. This is historical-place context, not a film-production record.

sources.title: Cleveland Landmarks Commission: Albert F. Janowitz
sources.note: The current municipal Janowitz inventory lists Madison Square Building, 7812–4 Hough Avenue, 1915, demolished. This is a compiled inventory entry, with no individual permit citation or linked building photograph. The database cautions that unsourced entries need confirmation. S30 independently reconciles the frontage address forms.

sources.title: Cleveland Public Library: Madison Square on Hopkins plate 6b, 1921 (revised 1924)
sources.note: G. M. Hopkins & Co., volume 1, plate 6b; CPL leaf 325, parent 392, G1399.C5 H62 1920 V.1. The original map labels Madison Square Building on the southwest Hough / East 79th corner, with Hough frontage numbers 7812–7828. It reconciles 7812–14 and 7820 at building level, without assigning an apartment entrance or establishing the full facade.

sources.title: National Park Service: Ebenezer Heritage Sanctuary
sources.note: Ebenezer Baptist Church at 407 Auburn Avenue, Atlanta; location visible in the opening funeral footage.

researchNotes.topic: Clark Avenue: demolition chronology and the supplied pier point
researchNotes.checked: October 18 follow-up: compared the supplied attribution with the actual indexed stills and the identified institutional or archival records.
researchNotes.found: County photographs document Clark demolition in 1984–85, and an ODOT inspection dates the I-490 crossing to 1990. The proposed pier coordinates fall on an industrial roof in the 2019 aerial, so they are not adopted. The film’s through-truss comparison remains probable.
researchNotes.remaining: An in-service roadway and skyline comparison is still needed to establish camera direction and the exact furnace. A separate remnant survey is needed before publishing pier coordinates or present-day access instructions.

sources.title: Cuyahoga County Engineer photograph: Clark central truss, cea0146, 1984
sources.note: Michael A. Fuerst, 1984; Cuyahoga County Engineer’s Photography Collection, Cuyahoga County Archives; Cleveland Memory item 129. A view through the central truss during deck demolition closely matches the haunched transverse frames and crossed overhead lattice in frame 658. The intact roadway, skyline and camera position remain unresolved.

sources.title: Bridges of Metropolitan Cleveland: unusual bridges, chapter 6
sources.note: The chapter gives Clark Avenue Bridge’s total length as 6,687 feet. Its preceding acid-fume/uranium corrosion passage concerns Harvard–Denison, not Clark. The chapter’s 1980 demolition statement must be read at section level alongside County Engineer photographs dated 1984 and 1985; it does not establish the final removal date for the complete crossing.

sources.title: Ohio DOT: IR 490 over Cuyahoga River, 2020 bridge inspection
sources.note: State of Ohio report for Structure File Number 1811991, inspection July 27, 2020. PDF page 2 lists Year Built 1990. This dates the I-490 valley crossing but does not establish that it immediately replaced every Clark Avenue traffic movement.

sources.title: Michael A. Fuerst: Clark Avenue river-span demolition, 1985
sources.note: Cuyahoga County Engineer Photography Collection, cea0824; Cleveland Memory cca/807. The archive dates the river-span demolition photograph to 1985. Together with cea0146 and cea0144 from 1984, it documents staged demolition in 1984–85; no exact final day is inferred from a year-only catalog date.

sources.title: Cuyahoga County: 2019 spring aerial check of proposed Clark pier coordinate
sources.note: The supplied latitude/longitude 41.472714, -81.681121 maps to the center of the inspected 2019 aerial export, on an industrial building roof.
